card.thesis: Under current rules, an identical mortgage on an identical house can meaningfully cut federal income tax for a high-tax-state couple and do nothing for a low-tax-state couple.
card.overturns: "Paying mortgage interest gives every homeowner a tax break on their federal return."

claim: Tax year 2026, married couple filing jointly in the 22% bracket, buying the median-priced new home sold in the U.S. ($410,700, 2026 Q2) with 20% down and a 30-year fixed loan at the latest weekly average rate (7.03%, week of 2026-09-24): the $328,560 loan generates about $22,992 of interest in its first 12 payments. Whether that interest lowers federal tax depends on the couple's state and local taxes (SALT), because deductions only help above the $32,200 standard deduction. With $5,000 of SALT (e.g., a state with no income tax and a modest property tax bill) the mortgage cuts federal tax by $0; with $15,000 of SALT by about $1,274; with $25,000 by about $3,474; with SALT at the 2026 cap of $40,400 by about $5,058 (all $22,992 x 22%). Any couple paying less than about $9,208 of SALT gets nothing from this mortgage's interest. The large value in high-tax states exists only because the SALT cap rose to $40,400 for 2026; current law sets the cap back to $10,000 for tax years after 2029, and at that cap (with the 2026 standard deduction) the same high-SALT couple's benefit would be about $174. Sources: 26 U.S.C. 164(b)(6)-(7), 26 U.S.C. 163(h), IRS IR-2025-103 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32).

assumptions: Tax year 2026; married filing jointly; both with and without the mortgage the couple itemizes only if itemized deductions exceed the $32,200 standard deduction.
Taxable income stays inside the 22% joint bracket ($100,800-$211,400) in every case compared (e.g., AGI about $220,000), and MAGI is below $505,000 so the full $40,400 SALT cap applies.
No other itemized deductions (no charitable gifts, no medical); SALT figures are illustrative totals of state/local income (or sales) and property taxes paid.

Home price = national median sales price of new houses sold (latest quarter); 20% down; 30-year fixed at the latest weekly national average rate; loan below the $750,000 acquisition-debt limit; no points or mortgage insurance.
State income tax effects are ignored; federal income tax only.
limits: Uses the latest published rate and price (not a history of outcomes and not a forecast). Actual SALT, rate, price and bracket vary by household; interest falls each year as the loan amortizes; the $10,000 comparison applies the post-2029 cap to the 2026 standard deduction for illustration only. No personal advice.
